name: VoiceBridge
oneLiner: VoiceBridge listens to a live conversation, from any source, and keeps one evolving, cited brief in front of whoever is handling it — who the caller is, what they want, and what to say next.
elevator: VoiceBridge's hero capability is real-time listening, not voice deflection: a listen session ingests transcript chunks from any source — realtime speech-to-text, a telephony webhook, a meeting bot, or someone typing — and returns one continuously refined, structured brief grounded in a Progress Agentic RAG (ARAG) Knowledge Box, with every factual claim carrying a citation. Every conversation is kept afterwards with its transcript, its accumulated sources and every version the brief passed through, so any two versions can be compared side by side, and retention windows purge the record on a schedule you set. The deployment is operated from inside the product: all 43 settings are edited on screen and take effect on the next request, access keys are named and revocable, and the ElevenLabs voice agent is configured and pushed to ElevenLabs from Settings rather than hand-copied into a dashboard. The same grounded pipeline is also available as a follow-on: answering a caller directly when nobody is available, and handing off by a deterministic rule rather than a guess when the knowledge base cannot support an answer.
heroMoment: a live conversation streams in as transcript chunks and one brief on screen keeps rewriting itself — topic, who the caller is, what they want, what to say next — with every factual claim carrying a citation, and a failed refresh leaving the last good brief in place rather than blanking it.

customer.headline: The right answer, while you are still talking
customer.subhead: Anyone handling a live conversation has to know what is true right now — not after the call. This listens as the conversation moves and keeps one short, evolving brief on screen: who you are speaking to, what they want, and what to say next, with a source behind every fact.
outcomes: Less time on hold. The answer appears while the conversation continues, instead of the person putting the caller on hold to go and look it up.
New people get useful sooner. Someone who does not yet know the knowledge base by heart reads what is suggested rather than having to know what to search for.
Fewer confidently wrong answers. Suggested answers are drawn only from your approved content, and a field is left empty rather than filled with something invented.
Handovers stop starting from scratch. Whoever picks up an escalation inherits the brief and the sources gathered so far, and the session's record is there for review afterwards.

You can see how the conversation turned. Every version the brief passed through is kept, and any two can be put side by side — what the system understood at minute two against minute eight — which is how a supervisor reviews a call without listening to all of it.

Your own people keep it running. Connection, limits, branding, retention and the voice channel are all changed on screen by someone in your team, and take effect immediately — no redeploy, no engineer, no vendor ticket.
customer.heroMoment: A conversation is underway. On one side of the screen, a single brief keeps rewriting itself as the conversation moves — the topic, who the other person appears to be, what they are trying to achieve, the points that matter, what to ask next and what to say — with sources listed underneath. If a refresh fails, the last good brief simply stays put rather than going blank mid-sentence, and says plainly that it is showing the last good version.
trust: It never speaks. Nothing is injected into the call — it puts information on a screen and leaves the conversation to the people having it.
Facts come from your content. The brief is built from your own approved material, and is written to leave a field blank rather than invent something.
Sources are always visible, so anything on screen can be checked before it is said out loud.
It fails quietly, not loudly. A slow or failed refresh leaves the previous brief in place, marked as the last good version, rather than flashing an error at someone mid-conversation.
Each session can be limited to what that caller is entitled to see, enforced when content is retrieved rather than filtered out afterwards.
You decide how long anything is kept. Retention windows for conversations, turn logs and quality runs are yours to set, with an immediate purge when you need one.

Access is named and revocable. Keys are issued and withdrawn in the product, a withdrawal takes effect on the very next request, and the record of the key survives its own revocation so the audit trail stays intact.
Changes are on the record. Every configuration change is written to an audit log with who made it, what moved and when — never the values themselves.
It can run inside your own environment, in your own country, or fully offline — and it is open source, so your team can read how every suggestion was produced.

faq.q: Is it fast enough to keep up?
faq.a: Yes, for this job, and we would rather be precise than impressive: the brief typically refreshes in around three seconds. Because it sits alongside a conversation that is still happening — rather than making a caller wait in silence — a person speaking for eight to fifteen seconds a turn leaves comfortable room. The same three seconds would be far too slow for an automated voice that answers the caller directly, which is why that is a secondary capability here and not the main event.

faq.q: Do we need a particular phone system or speech provider?
faq.a: No. It takes the words of the conversation from whatever you already have — a contact-centre platform, a meeting tool, a speech-to-text service, or a person typing. It does not provide telephony or transcription itself, which is deliberate: you keep the vendors you already trust. Out of the box it is wired to ElevenLabs for live transcription, the voice channel and an optional spoken cue, and it works perfectly well with none of that configured.

faq.q: Can it answer a caller on the phone as well?
faq.a: It can, through a voice agent — and the agent is set up from inside this product rather than by hand. The product works out what the agent should look like, shows you the difference between that and what the voice platform actually has, and pushes the change: the prompt, the greeting, the voice, and the address and credentials it calls back on. Setting up the second customer is a form and a button, not a second trip through somebody's dashboard.

faq.q: Does it listen to the customer without them knowing?
faq.a: That is your decision and your disclosure to make, in line with the rules that apply to you. Technically it is the same conversation your systems already have; it adds no audio and says nothing.

faq.q: Will it tell someone something wrong?
faq.a: It draws only on the content you have approved, leaves gaps empty rather than filling them, and lists its sources so the person can check before speaking. It is a prompt for a person, never an instruction, and the person remains responsible for what they say.

faq.q: What do we get to review afterwards?
faq.a: The whole conversation: the final brief, the full transcript, the sources it drew on, and every version the brief passed through with its timestamp and how long it took. Any two versions can be compared side by side, and the record exports as a document. Quality figures — response times, how often it handed off, how often a suggestion carried a citation — are kept across all conversations, not just one.

faq.q: How long is anything kept, and who can change that?
faq.a: As long as you say. Separate retention windows for conversations, turn logs and quality runs are settings in the product, with an optional automatic purge and a manual one for when a customer asks. Changing them is a screen, not a support request, and the change is audited.

faq.q: Can it appear inside the software our people already use?
faq.a: Yes. It has no opinion about where the brief is displayed — your agent desktop, case system or meeting tool can render it in its own interface. Everything the product's own screens do is available to a caller through the same documented API, and the product carries an explorer that lets a developer try each operation against a live deployment first.

faq.q: What about sensitive information in the conversation?
faq.a: Automatic redaction of personal data is not built in yet, so today it is managed by where the system runs, who can reach it and how long it is kept — usually your own environment, in your own country, with access controlled around it and a retention window set. Say early if redaction is a hard requirement.

faq.q: What does it not do?
faq.a: It does not record, score, coach or grade anyone, it does not measure talk time, and it does not connect to your CRM. It produces one grounded brief and nothing else.

cta.label: Watch it follow one of your conversations
cta.body: Paste in a real transcript and see what the brief would have shown at each turn. The launch video and the narrated walkthrough on this page show the whole thing first, if you would rather watch than book.

personas.title: Contact-centre supervisor / enablement lead
personas.body: Wants agents — especially new ones — to say the right thing on a live call without memorising the knowledge base, and to see afterwards what the call actually covered. Objects: "why is a self-updating brief better than a search bar my agents already have?"

personas.title: Sales engineer running discovery calls
personas.body: Wants to track what a prospect has said, what they're really trying to solve, and what to ask or offer next, without breaking eye contact with the call to search for a spec sheet. Objects: "does it keep up with the conversation, or is it one turn behind?"

personas.title: AI platform lead
personas.body: Wants to add a live-conversation copilot to an existing telephony/CRM/meeting stack without taking on a new STT vendor dependency or a bespoke integration per channel. Objects: "is the session API really independent of how the transcript arrives?"

personas.title: Compliance reviewer
personas.body: Needs to sign off a system that suggests things to a person on a live call, with evidence every factual claim traces to approved content, a retention window they control, and honest degradation when it doesn't know. Objects: "show me a suggested answer can always be traced to a citation."

capabilities.title: One brief, not a stream of alerts
capabilities.body: A single panel that is refined as the conversation develops, rather than a pile of notifications. The person reads one thing, in one place, and it stays current — topic, who they are speaking to, what that person wants, the points that matter, what to ask and what to say.

capabilities.title: Grounded suggestions with visible sources
capabilities.body: Suggested answers and recommendations come from your own approved content, and the sources drawn on during the call accumulate underneath the brief — so by the end there is a list of exactly what informed the conversation. Where your content does not cover something, the brief says nothing rather than filling the gap.

capabilities.title: Works with the conversation you already have
capabilities.body: It takes the words of the conversation from whatever you already use — a phone system, a meeting tool, a speech service, or someone typing — rather than requiring a new platform. Live transcription, the voice channel and an optional spoken cue are wired to ElevenLabs out of the box, and the product works with none of that configured.

capabilities.title: A record you can actually review
capabilities.body: Every conversation is kept with its transcript, its sources and every version the brief passed through; any two versions can be compared side by side to see what changed and when, and the whole record exports as a document for a handover or a review.

capabilities.title: Only the right person sees the right thing
capabilities.body: A session can be limited to what this particular customer or caller is entitled to, enforced when content is retrieved rather than filtered out of an answer afterwards, so restricted content never appears in the brief.

capabilities.title: It answers the phone too, when nobody can
capabilities.body: The same grounded pipeline can answer a caller directly and hand over to a person by a fixed rule whenever your content cannot support an answer. The voice agent behind it is configured in this product — prompt, greeting, voice and the address it calls back on — compared against what the voice platform actually has, and pushed with one action.

capabilities.title: Your own people operate it
capabilities.body: All 43 settings — connection, limits, branding and logo, integrations, retention, operations — are edited on screen by a signed-in operator, take effect on the next request with no redeploy, and are audited. Access keys are named, revocable and show when they were last used; a built-in API explorer runs any operation against the live deployment and hands back the equivalent command.

capabilities.title: You choose what is kept
capabilities.body: Retention windows for conversations, turn logs and quality runs, an optional automatic purge and a manual one — so a deployment holding real customer conversations can be made to forget them on a schedule you set.

howItWorks: A conversation starts, and the words arrive as they are spoken — from your phone system, your meeting tool, a speech service, or typed by hand.
As enough new conversation accumulates, your own approved content is searched for what is relevant right now — filtered, where it matters, to what this caller is entitled to see.
The brief on screen is refined rather than replaced: topic, who you are speaking to, what they want, the points that matter, what to ask, what to say.
Sources gather underneath as the conversation goes on, and a refresh that fails or finds nothing leaves the last good brief in place and says so.
When the conversation ends, everything is kept — transcript, sources, and every version the brief passed through, comparable side by side and exportable.
Your retention windows decide how long that record lives, and an operator can purge it on demand.
whyItWins: Only Google CCAI Agent Assist exposes a documented streaming, bring-your-own-telephony assist API a non-CCaaS customer can build on — and Google's is audio-first, grounded on Google's own knowledge bases (research/voicebridge-market.md, section b2).

Every other agent-assist incumbent (Cresta, Balto, Observe.AI, Amazon Q in Connect, Genesys, NICE, Talkdesk, Dialpad) is bolted to a CCaaS, a CRM, or sold as an integration project with no public developer surface.
Transport-agnostic transcript ingest: any STT vendor, any telephony webhook, any meeting bot, or typed text, through one session API.
Per-caller entitlement-filtered retrieval via session-scoped security.groups applied during retrieval, not as a post-filter — research takeaway #3; no agent-assist incumbent documents an equivalent.

The voice channel is configured from the product and pushed to the voice platform after a field-by-field diff — a repeatable API call per customer rather than a dashboard ritual someone has to remember correctly for the tenth one.

Operable by the partner who deploys it, not only by whoever built it: 43 settings live in the product, keys are named and revocable, retention is a window rather than a policy document, and every one of the 58 API operations is reachable from a screen or the in-product explorer.
Self-host on Apache-2.0 with zero runtime dependencies — no assist incumbent in the research offers this.

useCases.title: Live sales discovery copilot
useCases.body: An evolving read of who the prospect is, their goal, the stage of the call, and grounded talking points and product fits as a discovery call moves — the shipped demo's own sample conversation is built around this case.

useCases.title: Support agent assist
useCases.body: A person handling a live support call gets suggested, cited answers drawn only from the Knowledge Box, so a newer agent doesn't have to choose between guessing and putting the caller on hold.

useCases.title: Onboarding new agents
useCases.body: The brief acts as a continuously updating handrail for someone who doesn't yet know the knowledge base by heart — they read what's suggested rather than knowing what to search for.

useCases.title: Escalation prep
useCases.body: Whoever picks up an escalated call inherits the session's current brief and accumulated citations instead of starting cold.

useCases.title: Supervisor review after the call
useCases.body: The saved conversation carries the final brief, the transcript, the accumulated sources and every brief version with its timestamp and latency; two versions can be compared side by side to see what the system understood at each stage, and the record exports for a handover or a quality review.

useCases.title: One deployment, several branded customers
useCases.body: Each customer is an entry in the registry — its own Knowledge Box, greeting, voice, handoff line and brand overlay, edited in a form with the branding previewed live — so a partner can serve several of its own customers from one deployment without a fork or a redeploy.

useCases.title: Self-serve deflection
useCases.body: The same grounded-answer pipeline, without a human on the call, answers a caller directly and hands off by a deterministic rule when the knowledge base can't support an answer — with the voice agent itself configured and pushed from the product.

partnerModels.body: Deploy the accelerator as-is under the partner's brand, pointed at the partner's Knowledge Box — the fastest path to a live use case. Branding is configuration rather than a fork: environment variables give a deployment its starting identity, and from the full-implementation pass the product name, tagline, logo (uploaded in the product), colours, footer text, docs and support links and the "Built on Progress Agentic RAG" credit are edited in Settings, stored in the product and applied on the next request. An uploaded logo is served under its own locked-down policy and an SVG carrying active content is refused at upload. VoiceBridge goes further than the other two: the per-customer registry (greeting, voice, handoff line, Knowledge Box, model, reranker) carries per-customer brand overlays, edited in a form with a live preview, so one deployment can serve several branded targets. Honest caveats: the OpenAPI document deliberately keeps its own title, because the API contract is not the brand; branding covers visual identity only and is not multi-tenancy; and Apache-2.0 attribution stays in LICENSE and THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md whatever the credit toggle says.

Your existing application opens a listen session, streams transcript chunks from whatever it already has, subscribes to the SSE brief events, and renders the cards and their citations inside its own interface. The accelerator stays headless and never faces the end user: every screen it ships is a client of the same public API, and the in-product API explorer lets an integrator exercise each of the 58 operations against a live deployment before writing any code. Requires an HTTP client in your stack and somewhere in your UI to render a card and its citations. Completion signals today are SSE and polling; webhooks are a roadmap item.

Fork or vendor the accelerator and add a vertical: new throttle policies, new brief schema fields, new transcript sources, new trigger conditions, or another voice platform on the deflection path. Extension points are documented at docs/developer/extension-points.md and are deliberately small, pure seams (decideRefresh(), checkTurn(), the Collection<T> store interface).

Take arag-platform (STANDARDS.md, the ARAG client, the mock server, the HTTP toolkit, the UI kit and the product template via make new-product) and build a different live-context product on the same standards. VoiceBridge is the worked example for a listen-session/evolving-brief architecture.

faq.q: Is 3.3 seconds fast enough?
faq.a: Honestly, it depends which path. Per-turn deflection latency measures p50 3.3 s / p95 5.6 s, which is 13x-66x the envelope voice platforms design their tool calls to (Vapi ~50 ms, Retell <100 ms, ElevenLabs ~250 ms) — disqualifying for that path, and it cannot be streamed away, only papered over with a host's filler speech. In the listening path the same number is adequate because nobody is waiting for it: a human speaking 8-15 seconds per turn gives a 2-4 second budget (research/voicebridge-market.md, section c3).

faq.q: Which speech-to-text or telephony platform do I need?
faq.a: None specifically. A listen session ingests transcript chunks from any source — a realtime STT stream, a telephony webhook, a meeting bot, or typed text — through one session API. ElevenLabs is the default implementation of every voice surface (Scribe v2 Realtime for the microphone path, Conversational AI for the voice channel, text-to-speech for the optional spoken cue) while the contract stays vendor-neutral (D-32); with no ElevenLabs key the sample, typed and webhook paths carry the whole product. VoiceBridge does not do speech-to-text, diarisation or telephony itself; something upstream has to produce the transcript.

faq.q: How is the ElevenLabs agent set up?
faq.a: From Settings, not from a dashboard. GET /api/v1/admin/voice-agent diffs this deployment's desired agent and tool configuration against what ElevenLabs actually has, and POST /api/v1/admin/voice-agent/push writes the difference — the router prompt, greeting, voice, and the custom server tool's URL, X-API-Key header, timeout and body schema — merging into whatever ElevenLabs already holds so settings this product does not own survive. make agent-check verifies the integration against a throwaway agent and tool rather than a mock alone, which is how three live-API constraints were found and are now regression-tested: every request_body_schema property needs a description, a patch must not send both the deprecated inline tools array and tool_ids, and deleting a linked tool needs force (V-28).

faq.q: Is every setting really editable?
faq.a: Yes: 43 fields across six groups (branding, connection, limits, ElevenLabs, retention, operations) are edited in the product, stored in its own JSON store and effective on the very next request — environment variables are only the starting values. Secrets are write-only: set once, then reported as set with a four-character hint, and rotated the same way. A change that would break the turn-budget invariant is rejected and rolled back, connection changes drop the cached ARAG clients so the next call uses them, and every change is audited with who, what and when — never the values (V-26, V-31).

faq.q: How do API keys work?
faq.a: A real key store, not a shared environment variable: named keys with creation, revocation and last-used, where API_KEYS only seeds the store on first boot. A revocation rewrites the live key set so it bites on the next request, and the record survives its own revocation so the audit trail stays intact. Revoking the last active key reopens the API — the documented "no keys, no gate" behaviour, asserted by a test. Two honest notes: key secrets are stored in full in the deployment's own store, because the ElevenLabs tool push has to put a real key into the agent's header, and removing a key from the environment variable does not revoke it (the key list marks such a key) (V-27, V-33).

faq.q: Can we self-host it?
faq.a: Yes. Apache-2.0, zero runtime dependencies, Node 22.18+ runs the TypeScript sources directly with no build step, and it deploys via Docker or Fly or fully self-hosted. No agent-assist incumbent in the research offers self-host — it is one of VoiceBridge's strongest differentiators, though container/Helm/air-gapped packaging is still on the roadmap.

faq.q: What does it not do?
faq.a: No speech-to-text, diarisation or telephony. No coaching, scoring, sentiment or talk-time analytics, and no CRM or dialer integration — it is the brief and nothing else. It is not a Knowledge Box (retrieval quality is ARAG's job), not a durable horizontally-scaled session store today, and there is no automated quality gate for the live brief itself — only for the deflection pipeline. There is no avatar or video surface: the LiveAvatar and LiveKit routes were removed in the full-implementation pass rather than shipped half-built, because the bar is that an unimplemented capability leaves the product and the spec instead of appearing as "coming soon" (V-25).

faq.q: How is a caller's entitlement to see certain content enforced?
faq.a: Retrieval is filtered by session-scoped security.groups applied by ARAG during retrieval, not as a post-filter on results already returned. No agent-assist incumbent in the research documents an equivalent (research takeaway #3), which is why it is being made a documented, first-class session parameter on the roadmap.

faq.q: How long does onboarding a new customer take?
faq.a: A registry entry, a provision and a golden set — a form with a live branding preview, no redeploy and no code change, and the voice agent pushed from the same product. If a customer ever needs a code change, that is treated as a defect in the abstraction, not a one-off to work around.

faq.q: Is the product name final?
faq.a: No. VoiceBridge is the name in the repository, the binary, the Fly app and the running UI. Per D-15 naming does not block the MVP and is a display-string change whenever it is settled; legal trademark clearance is outstanding, and a white-labelling partner replaces the name anyway.

faq.q: How proven is this today?
faq.a: After the full-implementation pass: 337 tests at 98.8 % line coverage and 83 Playwright journeys, with live writes verified against the real Knowledge Box and the ElevenLabs integration verified against a throwaway live agent. Earlier live measurements still stand: deflection smoke 3/3 at p50 2.9 s, and a live listening session in which the brief reached version 3 with 12 source chips and a last refresh of 4.7 s (STATUS.md, 2026-09-12 20:40). The walkthrough recording carries a narrated talk track and 24 screenshots cover the new screens.
